research.notes: 2026 depth synthesis for paying many players efficiently. HEADLINE STATUS (verified 2026-06-14): the Batch transaction (XLS-56) is NOT mainnet-enabled. It was introduced in rippled v2.5.0, reached the amendment-voting phase, then a critical signature-validation flaw was disclosed 2026-02-19 (Pranamya Keshkamat + Cantina AI's autonomous tool 'Apex') in which a batch signer whose key matched its own account caused the validator loop to early-exit and skip remaining signers, allowing unauthorized inner transactions on arbitrary accounts. rippled v3.1.1 (2026-02-23) marked both Batch and fixBatchInnerSigs as UNSUPPORTED/Obsolete so they can no longer receive validator votes; the known-amendments page now shows Batch status 'Obsolete' with note 'disabled in v3.1.1 due to a bug; will be replaced by BatchV1_1 in a future release.' Batch was never live on Mainnet and no funds were ever at risk. BatchV1_1 (the corrected re-introduction) is under review with no release date as of mid-2026. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR A STUDIO DOING MASS PAYOUTS TODAY: you CANNOT rely on atomic on-ledger batching on mainnet right now. The production-proven pattern for high-throughput reward distribution in mid-2026 is one Payment per player, parallelized via Tickets (out-of-order/concurrent submission, up to 250 reserved sequence numbers) and gated by sequence/fee/queue management with idempotent retry keyed on tx hash + LastLedgerSequence. Design the payout service so a future flip to BatchV1_1 is a swap of the submission layer, not the accounting layer. Fee math is the floor cost not the spend driver: base reference cost is ~10 drops (0.00001 XRP) per Payment under no load, escalating exponentially when the open-ledger target is exceeded; the queue holds at most 10 txns per sending account, so a single hot payout account is a throughput bottleneck — shard across multiple funded payout accounts and/or pace submission to the open-ledger cost.

capabilities.name: Batch transaction (XLS-56)
capabilities.network_status: NOT enabled on Mainnet. Status 'Obsolete'. Introduced in rippled v2.5.0, reached amendment voting, then disabled in v3.1.1 (2026-02-23) after a critical signature-validation vulnerability disclosed 2026-02-19. Marked unsupported so it can no longer be voted in. Never live on Mainnet. To be replaced by BatchV1_1 (in review, no release date as of mid-2026).
capabilities.summary: A single outer Batch transaction that wraps 2-8 inner ('raw') transactions and applies them atomically under one of four modes. It is the canonical on-ledger primitive for atomic multi-send / multi-step flows, and would be the natural fit for paying many players in one signed envelope. CRITICAL: it is not usable on Mainnet in mid-2026 — the original amendment was found to have a signature-validation early-exit bug (a signer whose key matched its own account short-circuited the loop, skipping validation of remaining signers and allowing unauthorized inner transactions on arbitrary accounts), so it was disabled in rippled v3.1.1 and is awaiting a corrected re-introduction as BatchV1_1. Build payout architecture so that batching is an optional acceleration layer to be enabled when BatchV1_1 ships, not a hard dependency today.

key_fields.modes: ALLORNOTHING (0x00010000) — all inner txns must succeed or none apply; ONLYONE (0x00020000) — only the first inner txn that would succeed is applied, rest skipped; UNTILFAILURE (0x00040000) — apply in order until the first failure, then stop; INDEPENDENT (0x00080000) — apply all inner txns regardless of individual failures
key_fields.RawTransactions: Array of 2-8 inner transactions. Each inner txn MUST carry the tfInnerBatchTxn flag (0x40000000), set Fee to '0', have an empty SigningPubKey and NO TxnSignature, and omit any Signers field.
key_fields.BatchSigners: Array enabling multi-account batches; each entry has Account plus either SigningPubKey/TxnSignature (single-sign) or a Signers field (multi-sign). This is the surface where the disclosed vulnerability lived.
key_fields.atomicity: Inner-txn outcomes are governed entirely by the chosen mode; per-inner metadata is stored separately for backward compatibility. For reward payouts INDEPENDENT mimics 'fire all, ignore stragglers'; ALLORNOTHING gives true all-or-nothing semantics.
key_fields.fee_model: Outer fee = (n + 2) * base_fee + sum of the inner transactions' fees, where n is the number of batch signatures. Inner Fee fields are '0'; the cost is rolled up into the outer transaction.
key_fields.inner_tx_limit: 2 to 8 inner transactions per Batch (small — Batch is for atomicity, not bulk throughput; thousands of payouts still need many Batches or many individual sends)

capabilities.gotchas: Do NOT design a mid-2026 mass-payout system that depends on Batch — it is blocked on Mainnet and there is no shipping replacement yet. Even when BatchV1_1 lands, the inner-tx cap is only 8, so Batch is an atomicity tool (e.g. 'pay-and-clawback' or 'swap-and-pay' pairs), not a bulk-throughput tool; paying 10,000 players still means thousands of envelopes. The four flags are mutually exclusive — pick exactly one mode. Inner transactions with a non-zero Fee, a signature, or a missing tfInnerBatchTxn flag are malformed. Track BatchV1_1 on the known-amendments page before writing any code against it; the field/flag shapes may shift in the re-spec.

best_for.purpose: Atomic all-or-nothing multi-step payout (when BatchV1_1 ships)
Paired economic actions e.g. mint-and-pay or swap-and-distribute
Bulk reward distribution to thousands of players

capabilities.name: Tickets (out-of-order sequence reservation)
capabilities.network_status: Enabled on Mainnet (TicketBatch amendment, long-live). Production-stable and the load-bearing primitive for parallel mass payouts in mid-2026 given Batch is blocked.
capabilities.summary: A Ticket reserves a sequence number in advance so a later transaction can be submitted out of normal sequence order by setting TicketSequence instead of Sequence. This is THE mechanism that makes concurrent payout submission safe today: with Batch blocked, a payout service pre-reserves a block of Tickets (one TicketCreate makes up to 250), then fires many Payments in parallel — each pinned to its own Ticket — without serializing on the account's single advancing Sequence number. Because each send consumes exactly one Ticket and does not touch the normal sequence, retries and reordering are deterministic and idempotent at the slot level.

key_fields.TicketCreate: One signed transaction reserves up to 250 sequence numbers as Tickets at once
key_fields.max_tickets: An account may hold at most 250 Tickets in the ledger at a time, and cannot create more than 250 at a time
key_fields.reserve: 0.2 XRP owner reserve per Ticket (each Ticket is a separate owner-reserve item); reclaimed when the Ticket is consumed
key_fields.TicketSequence: Set on a later transaction to spend a specific reserved Ticket instead of using Sequence; consuming a Ticket removes its Ticket object and does NOT advance the account's normal sequence number
key_fields.sequence_derivation: A TicketCreate sent with Sequence N produces Tickets starting at TicketSequence N+1
key_fields.parallelism: Different in-flight transactions use different Tickets, so they can be prepared/signed/submitted concurrently with no sequence-number contention

capabilities.gotchas: 250 is a hard ceiling on outstanding Tickets per account — to sustain thousands of concurrent sends you must continuously top up Tickets and/or shard across multiple payout accounts. Each Ticket locks 0.2 XRP of owner reserve until consumed, so over-reserving ties up capital. A Ticket is single-use; consuming it (even by a failed tec result) burns the slot, so your slot-allocator must track which Ticket each retry uses to stay idempotent. Tickets give parallelism, not atomicity — they do NOT make a group of payouts all-or-nothing (that is what Batch/BatchV1_1 would provide). The transaction queue still caps each sending account at 10 queued txns regardless of how many Tickets exist.

best_for.purpose: Parallel/concurrent submission of many independent player payouts
Reward-distribution job that must not serialize on one Sequence
Collecting multisig signatures on several payouts in parallel

capabilities.name: Parallel payout via Ticket pool
capabilities.network_status: Composed entirely from Mainnet-enabled primitives (TicketCreate + Payment). Production-viable in mid-2026; the recommended throughput pattern while Batch is blocked.
capabilities.summary: The mid-2026 reference architecture for paying many players concurrently from a backend: maintain a pool of reserved Tickets on one or more funded payout accounts, assign each pending payout a distinct Ticket, then sign and submit Payments in parallel. Because each Payment is pinned to its own Ticket (not the advancing account Sequence), submissions do not have to be strictly ordered and a failed/dropped send can be retried in its own slot without blocking others. A slot-allocator maps (player, payout-id) -> Ticket, and a refiller issues new TicketCreate batches as Tickets are consumed, keeping the outstanding count under the 250 ceiling per account.

key_fields.building_blocks: TicketCreate (reserve up to 250 slots) + Payment with TicketSequence per player
key_fields.concurrency_unit: One Ticket = one independently submittable, independently retryable payout slot
key_fields.throughput_scaling: Shard across K payout accounts to exceed the per-account 250-Ticket / 10-queue limits; aggregate throughput ~ K * ledger-inclusion rate
key_fields.idempotency_hook: Persist (payout-id -> Ticket, tx hash, LastLedgerSequence); a Ticket is consumed at most once, so a retry that reuses the same Ticket cannot double-pay
key_fields.vs_batch: Provides parallel throughput but NOT atomicity; if you need all-or-nothing, wait for BatchV1_1

capabilities.gotchas: This pattern does NOT give atomic group semantics — partial completion is normal and your accounting must reconcile per-payout, not per-job. Owner reserve (0.2 XRP/Ticket) is real working capital; size the pool to in-flight demand, not the whole job. The 10-txns-per-account queue cap means a single account cannot have hundreds of Payments simultaneously in the open-ledger queue — pace submission to ledger close (~3-5s) and/or shard. Always set LastLedgerSequence on every Payment so abandoned sends expire deterministically and their Tickets can be safely reclaimed/retried. Beware destination requirements (DestinationTag, trustlines/authorized for IOUs, account existence + base reserve for first-time XRP recipients) — a payout to a non-existent account or missing trustline yields tec results that still consume the Ticket.

capabilities.name: Open-ledger fee escalation & transaction queue
capabilities.network_status: Live Mainnet protocol behavior (FeeEscalation). Always in effect; dominates the cost and throughput model of any high-volume payout job.
capabilities.summary: The XRPL sets a soft per-ledger transaction target; once exceeded, the cost to be included in the current ('open') ledger escalates exponentially, and transactions that won't pay it are placed in a queue for a future ledger. For mass payouts this is the throughput governor: a flood of cheap Payments from one account will queue (capped at 10) and require rapidly increasing fees to jump the queue. Read open_ledger_fee and load_factor from server_info / server_state and set each Payment's Fee accordingly — pay the open-ledger cost to land this ledger, or pay the minimum and accept queueing. Sustained high-volume payouts should pace to ledger close and shard across accounts rather than fee-bidding into an exponential.

key_fields.base_cost: ~10 drops (0.00001 XRP) reference cost per standard transaction under no load
key_fields.escalation: Required cost rises exponentially each time the open-ledger target is exceeded within a ledger
key_fields.queue_cap_per_account: At most 10 transactions queued per sending address at once
key_fields.queue_ordering: Ranked by fee level (relative to the type's minimum), ties broken by tx hash ascending; same-sender txns ordered by Sequence
key_fields.priority_cost: To push your queued txns into the open ledger you must pay enough to cover the open-ledger cost of this txn plus all your prior queued txns — compounds with queue depth
key_fields.signals: server_info -> validated_ledger.base_fee_xrp, load_factor; server_state -> load_factor, load_base; use these to compute Fee before submit

capabilities.gotchas: Do not hardcode 10-drop fees for a payout flood — under load they will silently queue and may expire. Do not fee-bid blindly to win the open ledger; the cost is exponential and one account can only have 10 queued, so beyond a point you are throwing XRP away — shard accounts and pace to ledger close instead. Queue ordering for a single sender is by Sequence, which is exactly why Ticket-based parallel sends behave better than Sequence-based ones under contention. A txn whose LastLedgerSequence passes while queued is dropped — always set it so failures are deterministic.

capabilities.name: Sequence vs Ticket submission management
capabilities.network_status: Live Mainnet behavior. Core mechanics for serializing or parallelizing sends from one account.
capabilities.summary: Every transaction from an account consumes either the account's monotonically increasing Sequence number OR a reserved Ticket (via TicketSequence). Sequence forces strict ordering — txn N+1 cannot apply before N — which is a hard serialization bottleneck for payouts: one stuck or slow send blocks everything behind it. Tickets break that dependency, letting each payout advance independently. Choosing Sequence for a few ordered admin txns and Tickets for the parallel payout fan-out is the central design decision in a high-throughput sender.

key_fields.Sequence: Per-account counter; each non-Ticket txn must use the next value, enforcing strict in-order application
key_fields.TicketSequence: Spends a pre-reserved Ticket; does not advance Sequence, so multiple Ticket txns are mutually independent
key_fields.head-of-line_blocking: A queued/stuck low-Sequence txn blocks all higher-Sequence txns from the same account until it clears or expires
key_fields.concurrency_model: Tickets convert a strictly-ordered stream into a set of independent slots safe for parallel submission and per-slot retry
key_fields.local_tracking: High-throughput senders track next-Sequence and the free-Ticket set client-side to avoid terPRE_SEQ / tefPAST_SEQ from racing submissions

capabilities.gotchas: Mixing Sequence-based and Ticket-based sends carelessly causes ordering surprises — a Sequence txn submitted while many Ticket txns are in flight still slots by Sequence. Submitting two txns with the same Sequence from racing workers makes one fail (tefPAST_SEQ) — for any parallelism use Tickets, not optimistic Sequence increments. Re-reading Sequence from the network mid-flood is racy; maintain it locally and reconcile against validated ledgers. Don't forget consumed Tickets free their reserve; a long-running service must refill Tickets to keep the parallel pool full.

capabilities.name: Idempotent retry on transaction results (tem/tef/ter/tec)
capabilities.network_status: Live Mainnet result-code semantics. Always in effect; the correctness backbone of any payout retry loop.
capabilities.summary: Reliable mass payouts hinge on routing each transaction result to the correct retry decision, and on a LastLedgerSequence + tx-hash idempotency key so a retry can never double-pay. The five result classes have distinct meanings: tes = success; tec = applied-and-charged-but-failed (a ledger change happened, the fee was burned — do NOT retry, the slot/Sequence is consumed); ter = not-yet-applied, provisionally retried by the server, may succeed in a later ledger; tef = failed and cannot succeed in any future ledger (e.g. tefPAST_SEQ) — do NOT resubmit as-is; tem = malformed, will never succeed — fix the transaction, never blind-retry. The safe pattern: submit with a known LastLedgerSequence, poll for a validated result, and only consider a payout 'unsent' (eligible for a fresh attempt on a new Ticket/Sequence) once the original LastLedgerSequence has definitively passed without inclusion.

key_fields.tes: tesSUCCESS — applied successfully; final once validated
key_fields.tec: Applied to a ledger to charge the cost and possibly other side effects, but the intended action failed; NOT retried (retry would likely repeat); Sequence/Ticket consumed
key_fields.ter: Not yet applied; server may auto-retry; could succeed in a future ledger (e.g. terQUEUED, terPRE_SEQ) — wait, do not resubmit a duplicate
key_fields.tef: Failed, not in a ledger, but could have succeeded in some theoretical ledger; typically can no longer succeed in any future ledger (e.g. tefPAST_SEQ, tefMAX_LEDGER) — treat as terminal for that submission
key_fields.tem: Malformed; cannot succeed under protocol rules; never applied — fix and rebuild, do not retry verbatim
key_fields.idempotency_key: Validated tx hash + the txn's LastLedgerSequence; a payout is only re-eligible after that ledger passes with no inclusion
key_fields.finality_rule: A submitted-but-unconfirmed txn is NOT safe to replace until its LastLedgerSequence is in the past (then it can never be included)

capabilities.gotchas: Never resubmit on a tec — it already consumed the fee and the sequence slot; treat it as a (failed) outcome and reconcile, do not pay again. Never blind-retry a tem (malformed will fail identically) or a tef (terminal). The dangerous case is timeout/no-response: if you resubmit before LastLedgerSequence has passed, the original could still land and you double-pay — gate every replacement on definitive LastLedgerSequence expiry. terQUEUED/terPRE_SEQ are NOT failures — they mean wait. Always set LastLedgerSequence on every payout so 'is it still possibly going to land?' has a deterministic answer. xrpl.js submitAndWait / xrpl-py autofill encode much of this; understand it even when using the helper.

capabilities.name: Reward-distribution architecture: per-tx vs batched
capabilities.network_status: Architectural guidance grounded in mid-2026 Mainnet reality (Batch blocked; Tickets + Payment live). Actionable today.
capabilities.summary: The mid-2026 answer to 'one Payment per player vs one batched envelope' for a studio is: one Payment per player, parallelized via Tickets, behind an idempotent payout service — because atomic on-ledger Batch (XLS-56) is NOT available on Mainnet and even BatchV1_1 caps inner txns at 8. Structure the service in two layers: (1) an accounting/ledger of intended payouts (player, amount, currency, payout-id, status) that is the source of truth and is currency-agnostic to the submission mechanism; (2) a submission layer that maps each pending payout to a Ticket, fees it to the open-ledger cost, submits, and updates status by validated result. This separation means flipping to BatchV1_1 later (to batch small atomic groups) changes only the submission layer. Cost is dominated by destination/reserve concerns and pacing, not the ~10-drop base fee.

key_fields.decision_mid_2026: Per-player Payment + Ticket parallelism is the only production-viable high-throughput option; batched-atomic is unavailable
key_fields.layering: Accounting layer (intent + status, source of truth) decoupled from submission layer (Ticket allocation, fee, submit, result-handling)
key_fields.cost_math: ~10 drops base/Payment under no load (10k payouts ~= 0.1 XRP in base fees, trivial); real costs are recipient base reserve for new XRP accounts and 0.2 XRP/Ticket working capital, plus escalated fees if you flood
key_fields.atomicity_tradeoff: Per-tx = no all-or-nothing (reconcile partials); future BatchV1_1 = atomic groups of <=8 only
key_fields.scaling: Shard across K payout accounts to beat the 10-queue / 250-Ticket per-account caps; pace to ledger close (~3-5s) to avoid fee escalation
key_fields.audit: Persist tx hash + LastLedgerSequence per payout for reconciliation and idempotency

capabilities.gotchas: Do not architect around Batch today — it is blocked, and BatchV1_1 has no release date and only batches <=8. Do not assume base fees are the cost driver; they are negligible — the spend that bites is recipient base reserve (a first-time XRP recipient needs the account-reserve to exist) and Ticket owner-reserve capital. For IOU/token rewards, the recipient must hold a (possibly authorized) trustline or the Payment tecs — pre-flight check trustlines. Build reconciliation for partial completion as a first-class state, not an error path, since per-tx payouts are not atomic. Keep the submission layer swappable so BatchV1_1 (or a future bulk primitive) is a drop-in, not a rewrite.

research.notes: Depth synthesis verified mid-2026 against xrpl.org and XRPLF. XRPL payment channels are the protocol primitive for streaming/high-frequency micropayments: the source escrows XRP on-ledger once (PaymentChannelCreate), then issues an unbounded stream of OFF-LEDGER signed Claims authorizing a CUMULATIVE drops total. The receiver verifies each Claim locally (signature-only, no consensus round-trip) and redeems the largest one on-ledger whenever it chooses (PaymentChannelClaim) — 'sign many, settle once'. Throughput is bounded by signature speed (Ed25519 ~100k sign/s, ~70k verify/s on commodity hardware), not by the 3-5s ledger close, which is why channels beat per-tx payments for tipping, pay-per-call, pay-per-second-of-stream, and pay-per-asset-chunk. Two structural constraints are load-bearing as of mid-2026: (1) channels are UNIDIRECTIONAL (source->destination only; bidirectional flow requires two channels), and (2) channels are XRP-ONLY on mainnet — token-enabled PayChan (alongside the XLS-34 token-escrow line) remains in spec phase with no mainnet amendment, so any IOU/MPT/stablecoin micropayment design must use XRP rails or a different mechanism today. Core PayChan amendment has been live since 2017-03-30; fixPayChanCancelAfter activated ~2025-08-29 (rejects PaymentChannelCreate with a past CancelAfter, returning tecEXPIRED). Each channel costs one owner-reserve item (0.2 XRP since the 2024-12-02 reserve reduction) plus the escrowed Amount, which is locked until claimed or returned. Safety hinges on SettleDelay (the dispute-window the source must wait through before a forced close completes) and on watchtower-style redemption (the receiver must redeem outstanding Claims before the channel can close, or lose them).

capabilities.name: PaymentChannelCreate
capabilities.summary: Opens and funds a unidirectional XRP payment channel from the sending account (source) to a fixed Destination. Sets the escrowed Amount (drops), the SettleDelay grace period, the PublicKey the source will sign claims with, and optionally an immutable CancelAfter. This is the one on-ledger setup transaction that enables an unbounded off-ledger micropayment stream afterward.
key_fields: Amount (XRP drops escrowed into the channel; locked until claimed or returned)
Destination (the only account that can receive from this channel; cannot equal source)
SettleDelay (UInt32 seconds the source must wait before a forced close completes if funds remain)
PublicKey (33-byte hex; secp256k1 or Ed25519 key the source uses to sign all claims)
CancelAfter (optional UInt32 Ripple-epoch seconds; IMMUTABLE hard expiry, cannot be extended)
gotchas: Unidirectional only: this funds source->destination; a return flow needs a second, separately-funded channel.
XRP-only: Amount must be XRP drops. There is no token/IOU/MPT channel on mainnet as of mid-2026.
CancelAfter is immutable once set — pick it carefully; only the mutable Expiration (set later via Fund/Claim) can change.
Since fixPayChanCancelAfter (~2025-08-29), a CancelAfter in the past fails with tecEXPIRED instead of creating then auto-expiring.
Costs one owner-reserve item (0.2 XRP) PLUS the escrowed Amount; both are locked, not spent.
Fails with tecNO_PERMISSION if the destination has DisallowIncoming set for payment channels.

capabilities.name: Off-ledger signed Claim (the micropayment unit)
capabilities.summary: A Claim is a tiny off-ledger data structure the source signs to authorize a CUMULATIVE total of drops deliverable through a specific channel. Claims never touch the network individually — the source sends them to the receiver over any channel (HTTP, WebSocket, in-band game protocol), the receiver verifies each locally, and only the final/largest claim is settled on-ledger. This 'sign many, settle once' property is the actual micropayment mechanism: throughput scales with signing speed, not ledger consensus.
key_fields: Channel ID (32-byte hex of the target channel)
Authorized amount (cumulative XRP drops total, NOT a per-claim delta)
Signature (over the canonical claim message, by the channel PublicKey)
Cumulative semantics: to charge two 10-drop items, claim #1 = 10 drops, claim #2 = 20 drops total
gotchas: Amounts are CUMULATIVE, not incremental — a new claim restates the running total; redeeming the largest supersedes all smaller ones.
Claims carry no expiry of their own; their validity is bounded by the channel's Expiration/CancelAfter and remaining funds.
A claim can authorize more than the channel currently holds — it only becomes redeemable up to the channel's funded Amount, so receivers MUST cross-check funding (see channel_verify gotcha).
Off-ledger transport is the integrator's responsibility; there is no protocol-level delivery or ordering guarantee.
XRP-only: a claim authorizes drops, never tokens.

capabilities.name: channel_authorize (sign a claim)
capabilities.summary: The rippled API method the source uses to produce a claim signature for a given channel and cumulative drops amount, using the channel's key seed/secret. The signature is computed over the canonical claim message — the prefix 'CLM\0' (0x434C4D00) followed by the 32-byte channel ID and the 8-byte big-endian drops amount — with Ed25519 or secp256k1. In production the source signs offline/in-app rather than handing a seed to a server.
key_fields: seed / secret / key_type (the channel's signing key material)
Output: signature (hex) the source ships to the receiver with the amount
gotchas: channel_authorize requires the signing key — never expose it on a public/untrusted endpoint; sign on the source's own infrastructure or client.
The signed amount is the cumulative total; mismatches between the signed amount and the on-ledger PaymentChannelClaim Amount cause the claim to be rejected.
Signing speed (not the API) is the throughput ceiling — Ed25519 sign/verify vastly outpaces secp256k1, which matters for high-frequency streams.
The 'CLM\0' prefix domain-separates claim signatures from transaction signatures; a raw signature over the wrong message will not verify.

capabilities.name: channel_verify (verify a claim signature)
capabilities.summary: The receiver-side rippled method that checks whether a claim signature is cryptographically valid for a given channel_id, amount, and public_key, returning signature_verified true/false. Critically it verifies ONLY the signature — it does NOT confirm the channel exists, is funded, or has that much XRP remaining. A safe receiver pairs channel_verify with account_channels to confirm live funding before treating a claim as money in hand.

Verification is the receiver's high-frequency hot path; prefer Ed25519 channels for throughput.

capabilities.name: PaymentChannelClaim (redeem or close)
capabilities.summary: The on-ledger transaction that actually moves XRP out of a channel, or renews/closes it. The destination submits it with the channel's largest signed claim (Channel, Balance, Amount, Signature, PublicKey) to settle accumulated micropayments in one ledger entry — 'settle once' after many off-ledger signs. The source can also use it to add funds, set/clear Expiration (tfRenew), or initiate closure (tfClose).
key_fields: Balance (cumulative XRP delivered after this claim; must exceed prior deliveries and be <= signed Amount)
Amount (cumulative XRP authorized by the Signature; must match the signed message)
Signature + PublicKey (the off-ledger claim; PublicKey must match the channel's stored key; required unless the sender is the channel source)
Flags: tfRenew (0x00010000, clears Expiration, source-only), tfClose (0x00020000, schedule/execute close)
gotchas: Balance must be strictly greater than total already delivered and no greater than the signed Amount, else the claim is rejected.
Destination redeems the LARGEST claim to capture the full cumulative total; smaller superseded claims need not be submitted.
Source closing with tfClose when funds remain only SCHEDULES closure — the destination still has at least SettleDelay seconds to redeem outstanding claims first.
Any validly-formed transaction touching an already-expired channel (past Expiration or CancelAfter) closes it and returns unclaimed XRP to the source.
Destination using tfClose closes immediately after processing the claim; source can only close-immediately when no XRP remains.

capabilities.name: PaymentChannelFund (extend funds & Expiration)
capabilities.summary: Source-only transaction to top up an existing channel with more XRP and/or extend its mutable Expiration, keeping a long-lived streaming channel alive and funded across many redemption cycles. Expiration (optional new mutable expiry; can only push later, never earlier than SettleDelay allows, and never past CancelAfter)

Topping up does not bypass SettleDelay for closing — dispute-window guarantees still apply.
Each additional Amount is additional locked XRP; it does not add owner-reserve items (still one channel = one reserve item).

capabilities.name: SettleDelay & closure / cancel mechanics
capabilities.summary: The trust model of a channel rests on its closure rules. SettleDelay is the minimum seconds the source must wait, after requesting closure of a channel that still holds XRP, before funds return to the source — giving the receiver a guaranteed window to redeem outstanding claims. CancelAfter is an immutable hard deadline; Expiration is a mutable soft deadline. Past either deadline, any transaction touching the channel closes it and returns unclaimed XRP to the source.
key_fields: SettleDelay (immutable grace seconds before a funded forced-close completes)
Expiration (mutable; set/cleared via Fund or Claim tfRenew; the soft close countdown)
CancelAfter (immutable hard expiry set at creation)
tfClose (source schedules close -> SettleDelay window; destination closes immediately after its claim)
gotchas: Choose SettleDelay long enough that a receiver (or its watchtower) can realistically redeem before funds revert — too short risks lost claims.
CancelAfter cannot be extended; a channel WILL die at CancelAfter regardless of remaining funds — size session lifetimes accordingly.
Since fixPayChanCancelAfter (~2025-08-29) a PaymentChannelCreate with a past CancelAfter fails (tecEXPIRED) rather than creating a dead channel.
After expiry, anyone can submit a transaction that closes the channel and returns unclaimed XRP to the source — receivers must not sit on unredeemed claims past the window.

capabilities.name: Watchtower / claim-redemption pattern
capabilities.summary: An off-ledger receiver-side service that holds the latest signed claim and guarantees on-time redemption — the XRPL channel analogue of a Lightning watchtower. Because a source can schedule closure (starting only a SettleDelay countdown) and the channel hard-expires at CancelAfter, the receiver MUST submit its largest claim before those deadlines or forfeit the accumulated balance. The watchtower monitors account_channels for closure signals/expiry and auto-submits PaymentChannelClaim in time.
key_fields: Persisted latest (largest-cumulative) claim per channel: channel_id, amount, signature, public_key
Monitoring: account_channels polling/subscription for Expiration/SettleDelay/CancelAfter and closure events
Auto-redeem trigger: submit PaymentChannelClaim before the SettleDelay window or CancelAfter elapses
Funding cross-check: verify on-ledger remaining funds (channel_verify checks signature only)
gotchas: Not a protocol feature — it is integration responsibility; if no one redeems before close/expiry, unclaimed XRP returns to the source.
Always store and redeem the LARGEST cumulative claim; redeeming a stale smaller claim leaves money on the table.
channel_verify alone is insufficient — pair with account_channels to confirm the channel is still funded for the claimed amount.
SettleDelay must be tuned to the watchtower's worst-case reaction + ledger-inclusion latency, or the window can close on you.
High-frequency streams mean the 'latest claim' changes constantly — persist durably so a crash doesn't lose the newest authorization.

capabilities.name: Channel reserve & XRP-only economics
capabilities.summary: Each open channel costs the source one owner-reserve item — 0.2 XRP since the 2024-12-02 reserve reduction — locked (not burned) while the channel exists, plus the escrowed Amount which is locked until claimed or returned. Channels are XRP-only on mainnet as of mid-2026: token-enabled PayChan (alongside the token-escrow line that shipped first) remains in spec phase with no activated mainnet amendment. This shapes the build decision: stablecoin/IOU/MPT micropayments cannot stream over a channel today and must use XRP or a different rail.

Escrowed Amount: locked XRP, returned to source on close/expiry if unclaimed

Currency: XRP drops only; no token field exists on the channel today
gotchas: Many concurrent channels multiply the owner reserve (0.2 XRP each) — batch recipients or reuse/refill channels rather than churning new ones.
Reserve XRP is locked, not spent; it frees when the channel is removed (only after close/expiry), unlike the per-tx fee which is burned.

XRP-only is the single biggest design constraint: if your micropayments must be denominated in a token, payment channels are the wrong primitive on mainnet right now — track the token-PayChan spec but do not assume it.

research.notes: Wave-4 depth synthesis (web-verified mid-2026). This lane is about the backend that sits between the XRPL and the game's player ledger: how value lands, how you authoritatively credit the right player, and how you reconcile without double-crediting. Four facts dominate the design. (1) Checks are PULL/deferred payments: a CheckCreate writes a Check ledger object that authorizes the Destination to pull up to SendMax later via CheckCash — funds are NOT set aside at creation (a Check is not an Escrow), so the sender must hold the funds at cash time or CheckCash fails (recipient may retry until Expiration). The Checks amendment has been live on mainnet since 2018 — battle-tested. (2) The authoritative result of a payment is NEVER the Amount field: read metadata.delivered_amount (aka DeliverMax in API v2), and the final TransactionResult from a VALIDATED ledger. delivered_amount is generated on-demand and is NOT in the binary metadata nor the metadata hash — it exists precisely so backends stop trusting Amount on partial payments. (3) Idempotency is structural, not bolt-on: an XRPL account sequence number means a given (account, sequence) signed blob can be applied at most once; combine a pinned LastLedgerSequence with persisting the tx hash + signed tx_blob BEFORE submission, and your credit key is the validated tx hash. tec-class results are INCLUDED in ledgers and burn the fee but do nothing else — they are final failures you must record, not retry as-is; ter/terQUEUED are retryable, tef/tem never made it in. (4) NET-NEW for 2026: the Credentials amendment (XLS-70) went live on mainnet 2025-09-04, extending Deposit Authorization with credential-based preauthorization (AuthorizeCredentials + a CredentialIDs field on Payment/EscrowFinish/PaymentChannelClaim). For a custodial/exchange-style game backend this changes the incoming-payment gate: you can now require KYC-style credentials on deposits without per-sender DepositPreauth objects. DepositAuth blocks direct Payments from strangers but pull-based delivery the receiver initiates (CheckCash, EscrowFinish-as-destination, PaymentChannelClaim, OfferCreate) still works — design custodial inflows around either a DestinationTag-required hot wallet or a credential-gated DepositAuth wallet. Reserve accounting is real money: every payment object the studio holds (Check, Escrow, PayChannel, DepositPreauth, trustline, offer) costs 0.2 XRP owner reserve on top of the 1 XRP base; a backend minting thousands of Checks/Escrows must budget reserve and reclaim it by cashing/cancelling/closing.

capabilities.name: Checks (CheckCreate / CheckCash / CheckCancel) — deferred pull payments
capabilities.summary: A Check is an authorization to PULL funds, not a transfer and not an escrow. CheckCreate writes a Check ledger object naming the Destination, a SendMax (the cap, in XRP or an issued token), and optional Expiration / DestinationTag / InvoiceID. Crucially, NO funds are set aside at creation — money only moves when the recipient submits CheckCash, and only if the sender still holds the funds and a viable path/trustline exists at cash time (otherwise CheckCash fails and the recipient can retry until Expiration). The recipient cashes with either Amount (exact) or DeliverMin (flexible: deliver at least this, up to SendMax) — never both. This makes Checks the right primitive for studio->player payouts where the player should claim on their own schedule (e.g. battle-pass rewards, tournament prizes) and for sending into a DepositAuth-protected wallet, since CheckCash is receiver-initiated and bypasses the deposit-auth block. CheckCancel removes the object: sender or recipient may cancel before Expiration, anyone may cancel after. Each Check costs the sender 0.2 XRP owner reserve until cashed or cancelled.
capabilities.key_fields: CheckCreate: Destination, SendMax, DestinationTag, Expiration, InvoiceID. CheckCash: CheckID (64-char hex of the Check object), and exactly one of Amount or DeliverMin. CheckCancel: CheckID. Ledger object: Check (LedgerEntryType). tec errors: tecNO_ENTRY (no such check), tecNO_PERMISSION (cashing account is not the Destination), tecEXPIRED (past Expiration), tecPATH_PARTIAL / tecUNFUNDED (sender lacks funds at cash time), tecDST_TAG_NEEDED.
capabilities.gotchas: Funds are NOT locked — a Check can be unfundable at cash time even though CheckCreate succeeded; never treat CheckCreate success as a guaranteed payout. Don't confuse Check with Escrow (Escrow locks funds and reserves them; Check does not). SendMax is a ceiling, not the delivered amount — for token checks always reconcile against delivered_amount from CheckCash metadata, not SendMax. Expiration is set by the SENDER at create time; after it passes the Check is dead weight occupying reserve until someone cancels it. A flexible (DeliverMin) cash can deliver less than SendMax if liquidity is thin — credit the actual delivered_amount. The 0.2 XRP per outstanding Check adds up for a backend issuing many; sweep expired/uncashed checks with CheckCancel to reclaim reserve.

capabilities.name: delivered_amount (DeliverMax) — authoritative credited amount
capabilities.summary: The single most important backend-safety field. A Payment (and CheckCash) can deliver LESS than its Amount — partial payments and flexible cashes are legitimate — so crediting a player from the Amount field is the canonical way to get robbed. The transaction metadata exposes delivered_amount (surfaced as DeliverMax in clio/rippled API v2), the exact currency actually received by the destination. Read it ONLY from a validated ledger result. It is generated on-demand for the API response and is deliberately NOT part of the binary metadata or the metadata hash, so you must request it from rippled/Clio rather than expect it in raw ledger data. For partial payments validated before 2014-01-20 it returns the string 'unavailable' and you must parse AffectedNodes balance deltas instead — not a concern for new payments but worth knowing if you ingest deep history. Rule: every player credit = delivered_amount from a validated, tesSUCCESS transaction, keyed by tx hash.
capabilities.key_fields: metadata.delivered_amount (string drops for XRP / object {currency,issuer,value} for tokens); aka DeliverMax in API v2. Returns 'unavailable' only for pre-2014-01-20 partial payments. Always pair with TransactionResult == tesSUCCESS and validated == true.
capabilities.gotchas: NEVER credit from Amount — that is the amount the sender was WILLING to send, not what arrived. delivered_amount only exists for successful Payment/CheckCash; for tec failures nothing was delivered (credit zero, record the failure). It is request-time-generated: don't expect it inside binary tx blobs, NFT metadata, or hashes. The legacy 'unavailable' sentinel forces an AffectedNodes fallback for ancient partials. Token amounts are objects, not numbers — compare on (currency, issuer, value), and beware issuer transfer fees already being reflected in delivered_amount.

capabilities.name: Reconciliation via transaction metadata (AffectedNodes + result codes)
capabilities.summary: Authoritative reconciliation reads the full metadata of a VALIDATED transaction, not just the top-line result. TransactionResult is the verdict; AffectedNodes is the audit trail of exactly which ledger entries changed (CreatedNode with NewFields, ModifiedNode and DeletedNode each with FinalFields + PreviousFields). For a deposit this lets you prove the destination's balance node moved and by how much (the ground truth behind delivered_amount), confirm a Check object was created/deleted, or detect that a trustline was touched. The changes are FINAL only when the transaction is in a validated ledger version — query rippled directly (the tx method with validated:true) for authoritative results; third-party data APIs and exported DBs are explicitly non-authoritative. TransactionIndex gives the deterministic position within the ledger for ordering. Backends should snapshot AffectedNodes balance deltas as the immutable receipt behind each player credit.
capabilities.key_fields: metadata.TransactionResult; metadata.AffectedNodes[] -> CreatedNode (LedgerEntryType, LedgerIndex, NewFields) / ModifiedNode (FinalFields, PreviousFields) / DeletedNode (FinalFields, PreviousFields); metadata.TransactionIndex (zero-indexed position in ledger); response fields ledger_index, ledger_hash, validated, close_time_iso.
capabilities.gotchas: Metadata is final ONLY in a validated ledger — never reconcile off a proposed/current-ledger result. LedgerIndex inside AffectedNodes is a state-tree key (object ID), NOT a ledger sequence number — don't confuse it with ledger_index. Read balance deltas from RippleState/AccountRoot ModifiedNodes (FinalFields minus PreviousFields) when you need ground truth beyond delivered_amount. Querying a third-party explorer for the 'result' is non-authoritative; go to rippled/Clio. A tec result still produces AffectedNodes (the fee burn) — don't mistake fee-only changes for a delivery.

capabilities.name: Idempotent submission: sequence + LastLedgerSequence + persisted hash
capabilities.summary: XRPL gives you exactly-once semantics for free IF you use the account sequence number correctly. Each account has a strictly increasing Sequence; a transaction with a given (account, sequence) can be applied at most once, so a signed blob can never double-spend even if you submit it ten times. The reliable pattern: (1) fetch current sequence from account_info with ledger_index:validated; (2) set LastLedgerSequence to last-validated + 4 so the tx provably dies if not included by then; (3) persist the tx hash, sequence, LastLedgerSequence, sender, and signed tx_blob BEFORE submitting; (4) submit; (5) confirm by hash via the tx method, accepting only validated:true. If the result is txnNotFound AFTER LastLedgerSequence has passed, the tx is permanently gone — safe to re-sign with the SAME sequence, a fresh LastLedgerSequence, and possibly a higher Fee. The persisted tx hash is also your reconciliation key: credit a player once per validated hash and you can replay your whole pipeline without double-crediting.
capabilities.key_fields: Sequence (per-account, from account_info ledger_index:validated); LastLedgerSequence (set to last-validated + 4); persisted: tx hash, tx_blob, Sequence, LastLedgerSequence, sender, validated-ledger index; verify via tx method requiring validated:true; result classes tes/tec/ter/tef/tem.

Resubmitting after LastLedgerSequence passes must reuse the SAME sequence or you risk a gap that stalls later txs. A consumed sequence with a tec result means the NEXT payout uses sequence+1 — track this server-side or use Tickets for out-of-order submission. Never key idempotency on your own internal id alone; key on the validated tx hash. Fee escalation: under load a too-low Fee yields terQUEUED or drops — bump Fee on resubmit.

capabilities.name: Destination tags & InvoiceID for custodial sub-account crediting
capabilities.summary: The standard custodial/exchange pattern for a single shared hot wallet serving many players. A DestinationTag is a 32-bit unsigned integer carried on a Payment that tells your OFF-LEDGER system which player sub-account to credit — it has no on-ledger effect, it is pure routing metadata. You assign each player a tag, publish 'send to <address> with tag <N>', and on each validated incoming payment you look up the tag -> player and credit delivered_amount. Enable the account flag asfRequireDest (lsfRequireDestTag) so payments WITHOUT a tag are rejected (tecDST_TAG_NEEDED) — this prevents the classic 'untagged deposit, which player?' support nightmare. SourceTag identifies the origin for refunds/bounces. X-addresses bundle classic address + tag into one copy-paste-safe string (the tag acts as destination tag on receive, source tag on send), eliminating the #1 cause of lost deposits. InvoiceID is a separate optional 256-bit hash field you can stamp on a specific Payment/Check to tie it to one order/quest invoice for exact-match reconciliation.
capabilities.key_fields: DestinationTag (32-bit uint, off-ledger routing); SourceTag (32-bit uint, return/bounce routing); account flag asfRequireDest / lsfRequireDestTag (reject untagged -> tecDST_TAG_NEEDED); X-address (address+tag, single string); InvoiceID (256-bit hex hash on Payment/CheckCreate for order matching).
capabilities.gotchas: Tags have NO on-ledger functionality — they only matter to your backend, so your tag->player map is load-bearing and must be backed up. Without asfRequireDest, players WILL send untagged deposits and you'll have unattributable funds; turn it on for any shared custodial wallet. A 32-bit tag space is large but design your allocation (don't reuse tags across churned players without a mapping history). X-addresses are the safer UX but some senders/wallets still only accept classic address + separate tag — support both. InvoiceID is a fixed 256-bit value the SENDER sets; you can't rely on arbitrary senders to set it correctly, so use it for flows you control (your own payouts, signed orders), and use DestinationTag for inbound player deposits.

capabilities.name: Real-time inflow detection: subscribe streams vs account_tx polling
capabilities.summary: Two complementary mechanisms feed the backend. (1) The subscribe WebSocket method with an accounts:[<hot wallet>] argument pushes a 'transaction' message every time a validated transaction affects that account — this is your real-time deposit webhook. Each message carries validated:true, ledger_index, ledger_hash, close_time_iso, and the meta object, so you can credit immediately on a validated event. The 'transactions' stream is the firehose of all validated txs; 'transactions_proposed' adds unconfirmed in-flight txs (validated false/absent, no meta, only ledger_current_index) — useful for UX previews but NEVER for crediting. (2) account_tx is the polling/history method: paginate the full transaction history of an account by ledger range, the authoritative way to backfill after downtime or audit gaps. Production pattern: subscribe for low-latency live crediting + account_tx sweep on a timer (and after every reconnect) to catch anything missed during a WebSocket gap. Only ever credit on validated transactions.
capabilities.key_fields: subscribe: streams (transactions, transactions_proposed, ledger), accounts:[address]; message fields validated, ledger_index, ledger_hash, meta, close_time_iso; proposed-only: ledger_current_index, validated absent/false; account_tx: account, ledger_index_min/max, marker (pagination), forward.
capabilities.gotchas: transactions_proposed and proposed-stream messages are NOT final (validated false/absent, no meta) — crediting on them is a double-spend/rollback hazard; always wait for validated. WebSocket connections drop — on reconnect you MUST account_tx-sweep the gap or you'll miss deposits silently; subscribe is not a durable queue. The accounts subscription fires on ANY affecting transaction (outgoing, trustline, offer), not just incoming payments — filter on transaction type + that your wallet is the Destination. Run your own rippled/Clio or use a reputable provider; public clusters rate-limit and may lag. account_tx is paginated via marker — handle the cursor or you'll truncate history.

capabilities.name: Deposit Authorization gate (DepositAuth + credential-based XLS-70)
capabilities.summary: A compliance-oriented inbound gate for a custodial wallet. Setting the asfDepositAuth account flag (lsfDepositAuth) blocks ALL incoming direct Payments — XRP and tokens — from senders who are not pre-approved; the account can then only receive value it pulls itself. Two pre-approval paths: (a) classic DepositPreauth transactions (Authorize / Unauthorize a specific sender address), each creating a DepositPreauth object that costs 0.2 XRP owner reserve; (b) NET-NEW for 2026 — the Credentials amendment (XLS-70, mainnet 2025-09-04) extends DepositAuth with credential-based preauthorization: authorize a CREDENTIAL TYPE from a trusted issuer via AuthorizeCredentials, and any sender presenting a matching credential in the CredentialIDs field (now accepted on Payment, EscrowFinish, PaymentChannelClaim, AccountDelete) may deposit — KYC/AML-aware deposits without enumerating every sender. Critically for game backends: pull-based delivery the RECEIVER initiates always bypasses DepositAuth — CheckCash, EscrowFinish where you are the destination, PaymentChannelClaim, and OfferCreate still work. So a DepositAuth wallet can take deposits via Checks/Escrows/Channels even while blocking random Payments.
capabilities.key_fields: Account flag asfDepositAuth (SetFlag value 9 / lsfDepositAuth, check Flags & 0x01000000); DepositPreauth tx fields Authorize / Unauthorize (-> DepositPreauth ledger object, 0.2 XRP reserve); XLS-70 AuthorizeCredentials / UnauthorizeCredentials; CredentialIDs field on Payment/EscrowFinish/PaymentChannelClaim/AccountDelete; bypassed by CheckCash, EscrowFinish (as destination), PaymentChannelClaim, OfferCreate.
capabilities.gotchas: DepositAuth blocks tokens too, not just XRP — turning it on can silently break expected inbound flows; whitelist before you flip it. Each per-sender DepositPreauth object costs 0.2 XRP reserve, so address-by-address preauth scales poorly — credential-based (XLS-70) is the answer for many senders. There's an exception: an account below its reserve can still receive up to a small amount of XRP to bootstrap. Credentials require a trusted ISSUER you've authorized and have their own expiration/validity — design issuer trust + revocation. This is heavier than DestinationTag-required for most game deposit flows; reach for it only when you need a compliance/whitelist gate, not for routine player deposits.

capabilities.name: Owner reserve accounting for payment objects (Checks/Escrows/Channels/Preauth)
capabilities.summary: Every payment-related ledger object the studio's accounts OWN is collateralized by locked XRP it cannot spend until the object is removed. Current mainnet reserves: 1 XRP base reserve per account plus 0.2 XRP owner reserve per owned object. Each outstanding Check, Escrow, PayChannel, DepositPreauth, Offer, trustline, ticket, and signer list increments the owner reserve by 0.2 XRP. This is the hidden cost of a backend that mints many payment objects: a payout system holding 5,000 uncashed Checks has 1,000 XRP locked in reserve; an escrow-heavy quest system locks 0.2 XRP per outstanding escrow. Reserve is RECLAIMED when the object leaves the ledger — cashing/cancelling a Check, finishing/cancelling an Escrow, closing a Channel, removing a trustline. Budget reserve as working capital and run sweepers (CheckCancel on expired checks, EscrowCancel on lapsed escrows) to recover it. Reserve amounts are set by fee voting and can change; verify current values via server_info / server_state at runtime rather than hardcoding.
capabilities.key_fields: Base reserve ~1 XRP/account; owner reserve ~0.2 XRP per owned object (Check, Escrow, PayChannel, DepositPreauth, Offer, trustline, ticket, signer list). Read live values from server_info / server_state (reserve_base_xrp, reserve_inc_xrp). NFTs reserve per-page (up to 32 NFTs) not per-token. Some objects (e.g. larger Oracles) count as more than one increment.
capabilities.gotchas: Reserve is LOCKED, not spent — it reappears when the object is deleted, but until then it's unspendable, which can starve a hot wallet that's also paying network fees. Hardcoding 0.2/1 XRP is a future bug: reserves are governance-adjustable; fetch reserve_base_xrp and reserve_inc_xrp from server_state. A backend that creates Checks/Escrows faster than it cashes/cancels them will hit account-funding errors (tecINSUFFICIENT_RESERVE) — pre-fund and sweep. Trustlines also reserve (the holder owes it), so a wallet holding many in-game tokens carries reserve too. Don't forget DepositPreauth objects count — per-sender whitelisting has a reserve cost that credential-based auth avoids.

research.notes: Mid-2026 depth synthesis for an XRPL-payments game studio. The load-bearing safety fact: on a backend you must NEVER credit a player based on the transaction's Amount/DeliverMax field — that field is the SENDER's maximum, not what arrived. Always read the delivered_amount metadata field instead. This is the single most exploited integration bug on XRPL (the 'partial payment exploit'): an attacker sends a large Amount with tfPartialPayment set, the tx succeeds delivering near-zero, and a naive exchange/game credits the full Amount. rippled API v2 (shipped in 2.0.0, Jan 2024; v2 is the modern default — Amount was renamed to DeliverMax in tx JSON, with Amount kept only as a v1 alias) renamed the field precisely to stop developers from trusting it. As of rippled 3.x (3.0.0 Dec 2025, 3.1.0 Jan 2026) the delivered_amount metadata field and the Amount->DeliverMax rename are the canonical, current behavior. Cross-currency settlement is the studio's superpower: a single Payment can send treasury currency A and deliver player-preferred currency B atomically, with the ledger consuming DEX Offers and AMM pools along discovered Paths, auto-bridging through XRP whenever that is cheaper. The safety envelope is built from four fields working together — DeliverMax (ceiling on delivery), SendMax (ceiling on cost incl. fees/slippage), DeliverMin (floor on a partial delivery), and tfLimitQuality (reject any path step worse than the Amount:SendMax exchange ratio). Pathfinding (ripple_path_find one-shot / path_find streaming) is advisory only — never trust paths from an untrusted server, and prefer omitting Paths on simple direct payouts so a malicious indirect route can't be forced. Everything here is mainnet-live, native protocol behavior (no amendment gating except where noted).

capabilities.name: Cross-currency Payment (send A, deliver B atomically)
capabilities.summary: A single Payment transaction where the source currency (SendMax) differs from the delivered currency (DeliverMax/Amount). The ledger consumes Offers in the DEX and AMM pools along a Path to convert A->B, fully atomically: the whole conversion executes or nothing does (no partial state, no stuck mid-conversion). This is the core primitive for paying a player in their preferred token directly out of a single treasury currency. At least one currency in the pair must be a non-XRP token (XRP-to-XRP is a same-currency direct send, not cross-currency); a Path between source and destination must exist with enough liquidity.
capabilities.key_fields: Account (source), Destination, DeliverMax/Amount (currency+issuer+value to deliver — the delivery ceiling), SendMax (currency+issuer+value the tx may cost incl. transfer fees/exchange rates/slippage), Paths (PathSet of conversion routes; auto-fillable, must be omitted for XRP-to-XRP), DestinationTag (route credit to the right player/account).
capabilities.gotchas: Atomic does NOT mean exact-delivery unless you control the fields: without tfPartialPayment a cross-currency Payment that can't deliver the full DeliverMax within SendMax fails with tecPATH_PARTIAL (insufficient liquidity/quality) or tecPATH_DRY (no usable path). Liquidity moves between submit and validation, so a quote can go stale. Set SendMax explicitly — if you omit it the tx defaults SendMax to the delivered amount in the SOURCE currency, which for a true cross-currency send is almost never what you want and will usually fail. A non-XRP DeliverMax/SendMax requires the issuer field.

capabilities.name: delivered_amount safety rule (never trust Amount on a backend)
capabilities.summary: The non-negotiable integration rule for crediting funds: when processing ANY incoming Payment, read the delivered_amount field from the transaction METADATA — not the Amount/DeliverMax field from the transaction body. delivered_amount is the amount that actually arrived; Amount/DeliverMax is only the sender's stated maximum and can be wildly larger than what was delivered when tfPartialPayment is set. A game backend that credits players from on-chain deposits must gate on delivered_amount or it is exploitable. This rule is current and canonical through rippled 3.x.
capabilities.key_fields: delivered_amount (metadata field; same Currency Amount format as DeliverMax; the actual amount delivered). Special value: the literal string "unavailable" for some partial payments validated before 2014-01-20 — in that rare legacy case derive the real amount from metadata AffectedNodes. Also confirm the tx result is tesSUCCESS and validated:true before crediting.
capabilities.gotchas: This is the #1 XRPL integration bug. Reading Amount instead of delivered_amount is exactly the partial-payment exploit (see capability below). delivered_amount only appears in metadata of VALIDATED transactions — do not act on unvalidated/tentative results. For XRP, delivered_amount is drops (string); for tokens it is an object {currency, issuer, value}. The API v2 rename of Amount->DeliverMax was done specifically to push developers off the wrong field; it does not change this rule — you still read delivered_amount, never DeliverMax, for crediting.

capabilities.name: tfPartialPayment & the partial-payment exploit
capabilities.summary: tfPartialPayment (flag 0x00020000) lets a Payment succeed by delivering LESS than DeliverMax rather than failing when full delivery would exceed SendMax. Useful for legitimately clearing the maximum deliverable given available liquidity — but it is the mechanism behind the exploit: an attacker sends a Payment with a huge DeliverMax, tfPartialPayment set, and minimal real delivery; the tx returns tesSUCCESS while delivering near-zero. Any system that credits from DeliverMax/Amount gets robbed. The defense is the delivered_amount rule plus DeliverMin. Understanding both sides (when to send partial vs how to never be fooled by one) is core for a payments studio.
capabilities.key_fields: tfPartialPayment (0x00020000 / 131072). When set, delivery is reduced instead of the tx failing. Constraint: DeliverMin <= delivered <= DeliverMax, and total source spent <= SendMax. XRP-to-XRP partial payments are forbidden (temBAD_SEND_XRP_PARTIAL). delivered_amount in metadata reveals the true amount.
capabilities.gotchas: Two failure modes for the studio: (1) RECEIVING — never credit on DeliverMax; always read delivered_amount. (2) SENDING — only set tfPartialPayment when you genuinely accept under-delivery (e.g. returning funds / sweeping dust); for a normal payout you want full-or-fail, so leave it OFF and let the tx fail rather than silently deliver less. A successful tx result code (tesSUCCESS) says nothing about how much was delivered when this flag is in play. Do not pair tfPartialPayment with a fixed SendMax expecting exact delivery — that's the whole point of the flag being dangerous.

capabilities.name: Amount -> DeliverMax rename (rippled API v2)
capabilities.summary: In rippled API v2 (introduced with rippled 2.0.0, Jan 2024 — and the modern default api_version for new integrations) the Payment field formerly called Amount is exposed as DeliverMax in transaction JSON, with Amount retained only as a v1 alias. The rename is purely semantic clarity: 'DeliverMax' makes obvious that the value is a delivery CEILING, not the delivered amount, steering developers away from the partial-payment trap. When submitting, you supply either Amount or DeliverMax (never both); when reading, API v1 shows Amount and API v2+ shows DeliverMax for the same underlying field.
capabilities.key_fields: DeliverMax (API v2 name for the delivery-ceiling field; alias of Amount). Amount (API v1 name; still accepted on submit, still emitted by v1 responses). Rule: specify exactly one of Amount/DeliverMax on submission. Pin api_version explicitly in client requests so the field name your parser expects is stable.
capabilities.gotchas: The rename does NOT make DeliverMax safe to credit from — it is still only the ceiling. The actual delivery is still delivered_amount in metadata. Code that handled both api_version values must branch on field name (Amount vs DeliverMax). Sending both Amount and DeliverMax in one tx is an error. Library defaults differ by version, so explicitly pin api_version (PIN_PER_STEP discipline) so a silent client upgrade doesn't flip your field names underneath you.

capabilities.name: Pathfinding (ripple_path_find / path_find)
capabilities.summary: Pathfinding discovers viable conversion routes for a cross-currency payment: chains of steps that ripple through accounts (same currency) or trade across order books / AMM pools (different currency). ripple_path_find does a one-time lookup of candidate path sets; path_find (WebSocket only) opens a subscription that streams updates as liquidity changes. The discovered Paths can be fed into the Payment's Paths field. The engine searches for the cheapest paths but is not guaranteed to find the absolute optimum, and paths can include up to several intermediary hops.
capabilities.key_fields: ripple_path_find params: source_account, destination_account, destination_amount (what to deliver), send_max (optional), source_currencies (optional restriction). Returns alternatives, each with paths_computed and a source_amount (cost). path_find adds streaming follow-up responses over WebSocket. The Payment.Paths field is an Array of path arrays (PathSet); each step element may carry account, currency, and/or issuer.
capabilities.gotchas: SECURITY: never trust path results from an untrusted/3rd-party rippled — a malicious server can return deliberately bad/expensive paths to profit. Use your own node or a trusted provider, and validate cost against SendMax. Paths are advisory and can go stale between lookup and submit; the ledger re-evaluates at execution. For simple direct payouts, prefer NOT specifying Paths at all (let the default path work) so an attacker-suggested indirect route can't be forced. Pathfinding is computationally heavy — don't hammer it per-frame.

capabilities.name: Auto-bridging through XRP
capabilities.summary: When converting one token to another, the XRPL automatically routes through XRP (A->XRP->B) whenever that two-hop route is cheaper than the direct A->B order book. This happens natively during order-book matching (on any OfferCreate / cross-currency Payment) with no flag required — XRP acts as the universal bridge asset, deepening effective liquidity between thin token pairs. For the studio it means token-to-token payouts often get a better rate than the visible direct book implies, transparently.
capabilities.key_fields: No transaction field — auto-bridging is implicit in DEX matching. It triggers only for token-to-token conversions (a pair where neither side is XRP yet XRP improves price). Observed via pathfinding output / executed Offers in metadata rather than configured. (Note: XLS-60d DefaultAutoBridge is a standards-discussion refinement of bridging defaults, NOT required for this behavior, which is already native.)
capabilities.gotchas: Auto-bridging only kicks in when it lowers cost; if the direct book is cheaper it isn't used. It applies to order-book/AMM token conversions, not to same-currency rippling. You can't force or disable it via a Payment flag. Because it interleaves XRP hops, your realized rate may differ from a naive direct-book quote — always size SendMax and read delivered_amount rather than assuming the headline pair rate. AMM pools participate in the same matching, so effective routing blends order books, AMM, and the XRP bridge.

capabilities.name: DeliverMin (floor on a partial delivery)
capabilities.summary: DeliverMin sets the minimum acceptable delivered amount on a partial payment: the tx succeeds only if DeliverMin <= delivered <= DeliverMax (within SendMax), otherwise it fails. It converts tfPartialPayment from 'deliver whatever you can, even dust' into 'deliver at least X or fail' — giving a safe floor when you must allow partial delivery (e.g. liquidity may be tight) but refuse to settle below a threshold. Only valid when tfPartialPayment is set.

capabilities.name: Quality limits & slippage control (tfLimitQuality)
capabilities.summary: tfLimitQuality (flag 0x00040000) caps the exchange QUALITY (input:output ratio) of every path step a payment consumes: the ledger only takes conversions whose ratio is equal to or better than the implied DeliverMax:SendMax rate. This is the on-chain slippage guard for cross-currency payments — it refuses to fill the payment through expensive path segments rather than burning your whole SendMax on a bad rate. Quality is defined per path; the engine prefers higher-quality (cheaper) paths and tfLimitQuality enforces a hard worst-acceptable bound.
capabilities.key_fields: tfLimitQuality (0x00040000 / 262144). Reference ratio is DeliverMax:SendMax (the rate you'd accept if the whole tx executed at the cap). Pairs naturally with SendMax (absolute cost cap) and tfPartialPayment+DeliverMin (allow under-delivery at acceptable quality instead of overpaying). tfNoRippleDirect (0x00010000) is the related routing control: skip the default path, use only the supplied Paths.
capabilities.gotchas: tfLimitQuality bounds the RATE, not the absolute spend — pair it with SendMax for a hard cost ceiling. Without tfPartialPayment, a quality limit that can't be met just fails the whole tx (tecPATH_PARTIAL / tecPATH_DRY); with tfPartialPayment it delivers less at acceptable quality. The reference ratio is derived from your DeliverMax and SendMax, so those two fields ARE your slippage tolerance — set them deliberately. tfNoRippleDirect is a different lever (route restriction, not price) and is easy to confuse with quality control.

research.notes: Wave-4 depth synthesis on the XRPL escrow primitive (web-verified mid-2026). Escrow is the ledger's native deferred/conditional-value object: an EscrowCreate moves an Amount out of the sender's spendable balance into an on-ledger Escrow object that can only be released (EscrowFinish) or refunded (EscrowCancel) under conditions fixed at create time. Two release gates exist and compose: TIME (FinishAfter = earliest finish; CancelAfter = expiration/refund) and CRYPTO-CONDITION (PREIMAGE-SHA-256 only — supply a fulfillment whose SHA-256 hash matches the stored Condition). The single biggest 2026 change is TokenEscrow / XLS-85, LIVE on mainnet 2026-02-12: escrow now locks IOUs (trustline tokens like RLUSD) and MPTs, not just XRP. Path to live was bumpy — the amendment first hit ~29 validator votes in Sep-2025, dropped to 16 when a validator found an MPT transfer-fee/accounting incompatibility, was corrected by fixTokenEscrowV1 (shipped in rippled v3.0.0, Dec-2025), re-approved by 30 validators on 2026-01-30, and activated 2026-02-12. Token escrow carries hard rules that XRP escrow does not: (1) the token ISSUER must opt in — asfAllowTrustLineLocking (sets account flag lsfAllowTrustLineLocking) via AccountSet for IOUs; tfMPTCanEscrow (plus tfMPTCanTransfer) on the MPTokenIssuance for MPTs; without it EscrowCreate fails tecNO_PERMISSION. (2) Token escrows MUST carry a CancelAfter expiration (XRP escrows may omit it). (3) The token's issuer cannot be the escrow source. (4) TransferRate/TransferFee is snapshotted at create and applied at finish even if the issuer later changes it. Economics: every escrow is one owned ledger object = 0.2 XRP owner reserve held until finish/cancel (reserves were lowered Dec-2-2024). Conditional EscrowFinish costs MORE than a normal tx: 330 drops minimum + 10 drops per 16 bytes of fulfillment. Permission model is permissionless-by-design: once a time-based escrow is Ready (past FinishAfter) ANYONE can submit EscrowFinish and funds still go only to the original Destination; once Expired, ANYONE can EscrowCancel and funds return to the sender. There is NO identity/credential gate on finishing — design crank-bots accordingly and never assume the recipient is the finisher. Freeze interactions: deep-freeze / MPT-lock blocks finish but still allows cancel; clawback cannot reach funds inside a live escrow (must wait for finish/cancel). For a game studio this is the primitive for vesting team/treasury allocations in your own token, time-locked or secret-locked quest rewards, and counterparty-risk-free P2P trades — but two separate escrows are NOT one atomic transaction (the all-or-nothing Batch primitive, XLS-56, remains disabled on mainnet), so a crypto-condition shared across both legs is the closest you get to atomicity today.

capabilities.name: Time-based escrow (FinishAfter / CancelAfter)
capabilities.summary: The pure time-lock form of escrow: EscrowCreate locks an Amount that becomes releasable only on a schedule, with no secret to manage. FinishAfter sets the earliest moment funds can be released to the Destination; CancelAfter sets the expiration after which the escrow can be refunded to the sender. An escrow with only FinishAfter is created Held, then flips to Ready once that time passes — and in the Ready state ANY account can submit EscrowFinish, with funds always routing to the original Destination. This is the canonical primitive for deferred payouts where you trust the clock, not a counterparty: scheduled payments, time-delayed rewards, and the building block under vesting. Ledger close times have ~5s granularity, and you cannot set times in the past. It is the oldest, most-exercised escrow shape on XRPL (live since genesis-era escrow, semantics finalized by fix1571 in 2018).
gotchas: Times use seconds since the Ripple Epoch (2000-01-01 UTC), NOT the Unix epoch — off by 946684800 seconds. A raw Unix timestamp will silently create a wrong window.

Anyone-can-finish: once Ready, any account may submit EscrowFinish (it pays the tx fee). Funds still go only to Destination, but you may need your own crank/bot to actually trigger release — funds do not auto-release at FinishAfter.
Release/expiration effective times can drift ~5 seconds because they resolve against the most-recently-closed ledger's close time, not wall-clock.
CancelAfter must be strictly after FinishAfter; you cannot create an escrow with past time values.
Each escrow is one owned object = 0.2 XRP owner reserve locked on the SENDER until finish/cancel. Thousands of concurrent escrows = hundreds of XRP in reserve.
For TOKEN (IOU/MPT) escrows a CancelAfter is mandatory — a finish-only token escrow is rejected.

best_for.purpose: Scheduled / time-delayed payout to a fixed recipient with no counterparty trust needed
Time-locked quest or season reward that unlocks at a known date

capabilities.name: Conditional escrow via PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition
capabilities.summary: The secret-locked form of escrow: EscrowCreate stores a Condition (a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition), and the escrow can only be finished by an EscrowFinish that supplies a matching Fulfillment — the preimage whose SHA-256 hash, wrapped in the condition encoding, equals the stored Condition. You generate the fulfillment first (a type prefix + arbitrary, usually random bytes), derive the condition (hash + length metadata), and hand only the condition to the ledger at create time; whoever later learns the fulfillment can release the funds (still only to the fixed Destination). PREIMAGE-SHA-256 is the ONLY condition type the ledger supports — there is no on-ledger scripting, multisig-of-conditions, or arbitrary predicate. This is the gate that makes hash-locked / reveal-a-secret flows possible: cross-leg atomicity tricks, claim-on-reveal rewards, and the conditional half of HTLC-style settlement. Conditional escrows MUST also have an expiration so funds can't be locked forever if the secret is never revealed.
gotchas: A conditional escrow CANNOT be created without an expiration (CancelAfter) — 'it is not possible to create a conditional escrow with no expiration.' Always design the refund path.
EscrowFinish with a fulfillment costs MORE: 330 drops minimum + 10 drops per 16 bytes of fulfillment. High-volume conditional release is meaningfully pricier than plain payments.
Only PREIMAGE-SHA-256 is supported. Do not assume PREFIX/THRESHOLD/RSA/ED25519 condition types from the broader crypto-conditions RFC — the ledger rejects them.
The condition is public on-ledger from create time; keep the FULFILLMENT (preimage) secret until you intend release, or anyone watching can finish it the instant they see it.
Combining FinishAfter + Condition makes the escrow 'Conditionally Ready': it is Held until FinishAfter passes, then needs the fulfillment. Both gates must be satisfied.

Use a vetted crypto-conditions library (e.g. five-bells-condition) to encode the condition/fulfillment — hand-rolling the binary format is error-prone and a malformed condition is unrecoverable until expiry.

best_for.purpose: Release-on-secret-reveal payout (HTLC-style / claim code) to a fixed recipient
Cross-leg link to make a two-sided trade feel atomic (same condition unlocks both)

capabilities.name: TokenEscrow — escrow of IOUs and MPTs (XLS-85)
capabilities.summary: XLS-85 extends the native escrow object beyond XRP so the locked Amount can be an IOU (trustline token, e.g. RLUSD or your studio's issued game token) or a Multi-Purpose Token (MPT). Live on mainnet since 2026-02-12 (re-approved by 30 validators on 2026-01-30 after fixTokenEscrowV1 in rippled v3.0.0 repaired an MPT transfer-fee accounting bug that had stalled the original Sep-2025 vote). Mechanically the time and crypto-condition gates are identical to XRP escrow, but the asset is held by locking it on the relevant trustline/MPT holding rather than reserving XRP drops. This is what makes denominating deferred value in your OWN token real — vesting, conditional grants, and escrow-secured trades no longer have to be priced in XRP. Critical control point: the token ISSUER must opt in (asfAllowTrustLineLocking for IOUs; tfMPTCanEscrow + tfMPTCanTransfer for MPTs), so if you are the issuer you gate whether your token can be escrowed at all; if you are merely a holder you depend on the issuer having enabled it.
gotchas: Issuer opt-in is mandatory and per-asset: IOUs need the issuer to set asfAllowTrustLineLocking (account flag lsfAllowTrustLineLocking) via AccountSet; MPTs need tfMPTCanEscrow (and tfMPTCanTransfer unless the destination is the issuer) on MPTokenIssuance. Missing it = tecNO_PERMISSION on EscrowCreate.
The token's ISSUER cannot be the escrow source — an issuer trying to escrow its own token as sender fails tecNO_PERMISSION.
Every token escrow MUST carry a CancelAfter expiration; unlike XRP there is no open-ended token escrow.

TransferRate / TransferFee is snapshotted at EscrowCreate and applied at EscrowFinish even if the issuer changes the rate later — the delivered amount is net of that captured fee, so the recipient receives less than the locked face amount when a fee exists.
Freeze interactions differ from XRP: deep-freeze (IOU) or MPT lock BLOCKS EscrowFinish but still ALLOWS EscrowCancel; clawback cannot reach funds inside a live escrow (must wait until finish/cancel).
Destination must already be authorized for authorization-required tokens BEFORE finish — authorization cannot be granted during settlement.
Still 0.2 XRP owner reserve per escrow object PLUS the locked token; you need XRP on hand to create token escrows even though the value is in another asset.

best_for.purpose: Lock deferred/conditional value denominated in the studio's own issued token or a stablecoin (RLUSD) instead of XRP

capabilities.name: fixTokenEscrowV1 — MPT transfer-fee accounting fix
capabilities.summary: A corrective amendment, shipped in rippled v3.0.0 (Dec-2025), that repairs an MPT accounting error in token escrow: when an escrow unlocked MPTs carrying a transfer fee, the original code reduced the MPT issuer's locked-token balance by the GROSS amount (pre-fee) instead of the NET amount (post-fee), corrupting supply tracking. For a builder this is mostly context, but it carries one operating lesson: if you are issuing MPTs with a transfer fee and using escrow, your correctness depends on this fix being active — which it is on mainnet, but matters when testing against older devnet/standalone builds or third-party infra that may lag.
gotchas: Activation history matters for testing: a node or sidechain running pre-v3.0.0 rippled can reproduce the gross-vs-net MPT escrow accounting bug. Verify the amendment is enabled before trusting MPT-with-fee escrow math in any non-mainnet environment.
This is a fix amendment, not a feature you call — there are no new transaction fields. Its absence silently corrupts MPT supply on finish, it does not error.
Only relevant if your MPT has a non-zero TransferFee; fee-free MPTs were unaffected.
